f1b27e8192:
The guide's wording is short: "window management, drift/bloat prevention (tool-output pruning, compaction), isolation via subagents." Behind it sits most of what makes a long-running agent work or fail.

This chapter treats the context window as a budget you allocate. It shows, with token counts, how agent sessions grow and where the growth comes from. Then it works through every lever, in the order you should reach for them:

  • pruning at the tool;
  • clearing used results, client-side and with the API's clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit;
  • compaction, threshold and on-demand, server-side and client-side;
  • what summarisation loses, and how a persistent case-facts block protects it;
  • placement and the lost-in-the-middle effect;
  • drift detection;
  • sub-agent isolation;
  • scratchpad and state files;
  • retrieval versus stuffing;
  • recovering a session that has degraded.

Two turn-by-turn traces with token counts tie it together.
93466b0289: Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/16-context-engineering/ (run bash run_all.sh). Everything runs offline, using the shared fake client and ctxlib.py. That's a chars/4 token estimator plus the pairing checks the real API applies.
6560364a79:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 03 covers memory types, the memory tool, the six-step context ladder at agent level, and the basic shapes of clearing and compaction. This chapter points back to those sections and goes deeper on technique, parameters, cost and failure modes.

Chapter 13 explains tokens and windows from first principles. Chapter 15 prices them and covers prompt caching. Chapter 17 covers prompt wording and placement of instructions. Chapter 21 covers tool design.
0d823e015c:
Every call to Claude is answered from exactly what is in the window on that call, so the quality, cost and latency of an agent are set by what you put there, and in an agent the window fills by itself with tool results the model asked for.

Context engineering is the discipline of keeping that window small, current and well ordered: prune what tools return, clear what has been used, compact what is old while pinning the exact facts a summary would lose, put the important material where the model reads it reliably, and move verbose sub-work and long-lived state out of the window entirely, into sub-agents and files.
5a76f00a09:
At 3.8%, the sub-objective is worth about two direct questions out of 53. But the reasoning runs through agent, cost and tooling questions in other domains as well.

The typical stem describes a symptom that grows with session length. "After about forty tool calls the agent starts re-querying records it already has." "The summary says the customer wants a refund but the amount is gone." "Costs per conversation tripled after we added a log tool." Then it offers four fixes. One is a bigger window or a bigger model. One is a prompt instruction to "remember" or "be concise". One is an arbitrary cap. And one changes what is in the window. The last one is almost always right.

The same reasoning appears in CCAR-F 5.1 and 5.4: progressive summarisation losing numbers, case-facts blocks, scratchpad files, /compact. If you're sitting both exams, this chapter covers those statements too.
ea0d61965a: Context engineering got its name in 2025. But every technique in it has an older ancestor in systems design. Knowing the ancestors helps, because the trade-offs carried over almost unchanged.
43111428ae:
Memory hierarchies and working sets. Peter Denning's working-set model (1968) observed that a program, at any moment, uses a small subset of its pages. Performance collapses ("thrashing") when the resident set is smaller than the working set. The fix wasn't more memory. It was a policy for what stays resident.

An agent's window is the resident set. Tool results it no longer needs are pages that should be evicted. The facts it will need again are the working set, and they must never be evicted. Every clearing and compaction policy in this chapter is an eviction policy.
963cac0b7a:
Caches and write-back. CPU caches and database buffer pools taught the second lesson. Eviction is safe only if what's evicted can be recovered, either because it's still in the backing store or because it was written back.

In context terms, a cleared tool result is safe when the tool can be called again. A compacted conversation is safe only for what was written somewhere else first: a facts block, a state file, a memory file. Information that existed only in the window, and was then summarised away, is a dirty page discarded without write-back.
5d03a0aee7: Retrieval-augmented generation. Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI (2020) paired a retriever with a generator. The model could then answer from documents it was never trained on, by fetching the relevant passages into the prompt per query. The choice between "fetch what this query needs" and "load everything" is section 16 of this chapter. And it's older than LLMs: it's the index-versus-table-scan decision.
b7d1652ca3:
Lost in the middle. Liu and colleagues ("Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts", 2023) measured a U-shaped curve. Models answer more accurately when the relevant passage sits at the beginning or end of a long input than when it sits in the middle.

Models have improved since. Anthropic's own long-context guidance focuses on ordering (long documents first, the question last) rather than on the curve itself. But the placement lesson stands, and the exam uses the phrase (section 12).
aca3b4a983: Virtual context. MemGPT (Packer and colleagues, 2023) framed the window as main memory and external stores as disk. The model paged information in and out through function calls. Anthropic's memory tool (chapter 03) follows the same idea, with plain files.
6c3d6beefe:
The name. In 2025, practitioners started calling the whole practice "context engineering", to set it apart from writing a single good prompt. Anthropic's "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (September 2025) gave the working definition this chapter uses. Find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the desired outcome likely. Treat context as a finite attention budget with diminishing returns.

The same month, the API gained server-side context editing: clearing old tool results and thinking blocks. Server-side compaction followed in two forms, at a threshold (2026-01) and on demand (2026-09). Claude Code had compacted automatically, and offered /compact and /clear, since well before either.
95cbebb7af:
Chapter 13 explained what a token is and why a window has a size. Here the question is operational. What occupies the window on a call? Which of those things do you control? And how much room should you leave?

Everything the model sees on one request counts against one window:

  • the system prompt;
  • the tool definitions (names, descriptions and JSON schemas, plus any system prompt text the API adds for tool use);
  • every message in messages, including tool_use inputs and tool_result contents;
  • images and PDF pages;
  • thinking blocks from earlier turns that the model keeps;
  • the output this call will generate, including any thinking it does now.

Input and output share the window. If you ask for max_tokens of 32,000, those tokens are spoken for even if the model writes 400.
ec0dca5a6f:
At the time of writing, the current models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1) all have a 1M-token window by default, with no beta header. They can generate up to 128k output tokens per request. They're billed at standard rates for long prompts, except Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more. (Check the docs; these numbers move.) Older models such as Sonnet 4.5 have 200k.

A 1M window changes what is possible, not what is wise. A million tokens of input costs a million tokens of input on every turn. It takes longer before the first output token. And it gives the model a million tokens to attend over.

That's why the useful number in production is a working limit you choose. It sits far below the hard limit, and it's the point at which your context policy starts acting.
86c53ac8a4: Write the budget down as line items, exactly as you'd size a JVM heap or a Kafka consumer's memory. Example 01_budget_calculator.py does this for a support agent with a 200,000-token working limit:
202a42711c:
Three things in that table are worth noticing.

First, the fixed lines (system prompt, tool definitions, facts block, retrieval) are small. They're also the lines that matter most per token. The history line is huge, and by the time it's large it's mostly low value.

Second, the output reserve is real. A model running with extended or adaptive thinking may spend most of its max_tokens thinking, and those tokens come out of the same window.

Third, the only line that grows on its own is the history. It grows at a rate you can measure from traces (here 4,200 tokens per tool turn). Divide the free space by the growth rate, and you know how many turns the agent gets before something must happen. That number is the design input for every technique later in the chapter.
f62404c243:
Know the overflow behaviour precisely, because a stem may describe it.

If the input alone exceeds the window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error ("prompt is too long") on every model.

If the input fits but input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, it depends on the model. Models from the Claude 4.5 generation onward accept the request. If generation actually reaches the limit, they stop with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded". Earlier models rejected such requests up front, unless you opted in with a beta header (check the docs).

So a long-running agent on a current model can get a 200 whose stop reason means "I ran out of window mid-answer". The loop must treat it like max_tokens, plus a signal that the history needs work. Compact or restart from state, then continue (example 17).
f1164310b3:
Some models also know their budget. Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 receive automatic "context awareness". The API injects the total budget into the system prompt, and adds a <system_warning> with usage and remaining tokens after each tool call. That lets the model pace itself.

Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable don't receive these tags. For them, a beta "task budgets" feature lets you set an explicit budget (check the docs for both).

For the exam, the point is this. The model's awareness of its budget depends on the model. Your harness's awareness is always your job.
5654bc263c:
Estimating with characters divided by four is fine for design, and the companion does it. Production code should count.

The token counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens) takes the same model, system, tools and messages as a real call. It returns input_tokens without generating anything.

With context editing enabled, the beta counting call also accepts context_management. It reports both the post-edit input_tokens and context_management.original_input_tokens. So you can see what the server's edits would remove before you rely on them. A preflight check turns those numbers into a decision:
fca7b9838e:
Counting costs a round trip, so most harnesses don't count every turn. There's a cheaper pattern. Read usage.input_tokens from the previous response, plus the cache read and cache creation tokens, which are also input. Add an estimate for what you're about to append. Count exactly only when the estimate is within, say, 10% of the working limit.

In Java, the same check is a method on whatever bean builds your requests. If you already have a Micrometer gauge for heap usage, add one for "input tokens at last call" per session, and alert on it the same way.
7d300fea7e: A larger window looks like a free upgrade. So be exact about why "just send everything" fails. There are four separate costs, and they compound.
1c3f2096ca:
Attention is a shared resource. Each output token is produced by attending over every input token, so relevant and irrelevant tokens compete. Anthropic's guidance describes this as context having diminishing returns ("context rot"). As the number of tokens grows, the model's ability to recall and use any specific piece of it degrades. It happens gradually, not at a cliff.

A specific failure follows. A value the agent needs (an order id, a constraint the user stated) is present in the window, but isn't used. Forty thousand tokens of log output sit between it and the current turn.
8b80448747:
Cost is resent. The Messages API is stateless. In a loop, the whole history goes out on every turn. So a tool result added at turn 3 is paid for on every turn after it.

If each turn adds a roughly constant amount r, turn n costs about n·r input tokens. A run of N turns costs about r·N²/2. That quadratic is the arithmetic behind section 05's trace.

Prompt caching (chapter 15) cuts the price of the resent prefix to a tenth, but only while the prefix is unchanged. Context edits change it (section 08).
0e5e5a6e41: Latency follows input. Time to first token grows with input length, and every turn of an agent waits on it. An agent at 150,000 tokens of history is slower on every step than the same agent at 15,000, caching or not.
e6885234b0: The window is finite. Eventually the run hits the hard limit, or more often your working limit, and something has to give. If nothing was designed to give, the run is what gives.
ba2de8fb66: These costs explain why the exam treats "use the model with the larger window" as a distractor whenever the stem describes accumulation. A bigger window postpones the hard failure. It leaves the other three costs in place, or makes them worse.
396f5c451b: The objective names two failure modes: drift and bloat. Practitioners and Anthropic's own write-ups use a few more. Separating them helps you pick the fix, because each has a different cause.
a2a88e9f19:
Abstract arguments about growth are easy to agree with and easy to underestimate. Example 02_growth_trace.py runs one twelve-step support investigation twice, with identical tool calls. A customer, C-7781, says order O-55120 never arrived.

The agent looks up the account, lists orders, and reads the order. It searches the knowledge base, reads the refund policy, and checks the shipment. It searches carrier logs, reads the invoice, and searches the knowledge base again. Then it reads the credit rules, calculates a credit and opens a case.

The system prompt is about 2,000 tokens. Six tool definitions add about 1,800.
bfc1398e9a:
The unmanaged run returns raw tool payloads and keeps everything. The managed run applies three changes:

  • tools return projections, the fields the next decision needs;
  • results older than the three most recent tool uses are replaced by a placeholder;
  • the policy document is excluded from clearing, because the agent must keep consulting it.

Here is the trace:
41688670ba:
The unmanaged per-turn column only goes up. Every tool result is still there at turn 12. That includes the 20,000-token log search from turn 7, whose only useful content was one line. By turn 12 the request is 76,000 tokens. Perhaps 4,000 of those are relevant to "open the case with the right credit".

The cumulative column is what you pay. It reaches 562,000 tokens of input for a twelve-step task. That's the quadratic from section 04, made visible.
56c1d5515c:
The managed per-turn column plateaus. After turn 5 it hovers around 11,000 tokens. Each new result is small, and old ones are cleared as new ones arrive.

The step at turn 5 is the policy document (6,000 tokens), which is deliberately excluded from clearing. That's a cost you choose to pay, because the agent needs the policy until the end.

A plateau is the shape you want. Per-turn cost becomes roughly constant, so total cost grows linearly with the number of turns, not quadratically.
b47fa7b5e5:
Where the 80% came from. Roughly two thirds of the saving is pruning at the tool. Turn 2's order list is 600 tokens instead of 9,000. Turn 7's log search is 700 instead of 20,000. The other third is clearing.

That ratio is typical. It's why the ladder in chapter 03 puts pruning before clearing. The cheapest token is the one that never enters the window. And pruning also removes noise from the turn where the result is first read, which clearing can't do.
55bc08bbd7:
What the managed run gave up. At turn 12, the managed agent can no longer see the raw order list or the log lines. If it needs them, it must call the tool again.

That's the bargain. It's a good one when tools are cheap and idempotent. It's a bad one for a tool that's slow, rate-limited or non-deterministic, like a web search whose results change. That case is what exclude_tools and a facts block are for.
0f477fd9b3:
Most bloat in an agent comes from tools, and you write the tools.

A tool written for a human dashboard, or for another service, returns everything it has. A human can scroll, and a service can ignore fields. A tool written for a model should return what the next decision needs, a count of what else exists, and a way to get more.

The model can't ignore fields. Everything you return is read, paid for on every later turn, and competes for attention.
2d8a92381f: Example 03_tool_output_pruning.py shows the difference on an order search over 200 orders. Each order has line items, an audit block and a billing address.
61e6d8c151:
Each element of the fixed version does a specific job.

  • Filter parameters (status) let the model ask a narrower question. Otherwise it receives everything and filters in its head, which it does less reliably than a WHERE clause.
  • Projection returns the five fields that decide what to do next. Detail stays one call away.
  • Pagination with a total tells the model that 66 lost orders exist and it has seen ten. That prevents a silent failure, where the model concludes from a truncated list that an order doesn't exist.
  • The note names the follow-up tool. It's a cheap way to steer the next call.

The ratio here is 98 to 1. Ratios of 10 to 100 are normal for list-shaped tools.
a4834debb2: Logs and documents need a different shape. Their value is in a few lines scattered through many. Example 04_log_pruner.py turns an hour of eNodeB log, 4,157 lines and about 31,000 tokens, into this:
0317b1a1ae:
The pruner does four things, in order:

  1. severity filtering: drop INFO and DEBUG;
  2. normalisation: mask the varying number in count=3, so repeated messages collapse;
  3. deduplication, with counts and first-seen time;
  4. a header that states what was suppressed.

The header matters more than it looks. Without it, the model sees two lines and may conclude the hour was quiet apart from them. With it, the model knows 4,115 lines were dropped by rule. It can ask for a time slice if it needs context around 02:41.

Truncation without a marker is one of the anti-patterns in section 19. A file read that silently stops at 2,000 lines invites the model to reason about a function whose second half it never saw.
27fe218f8d: In a Spring service, the natural place for projection is a response record per tool, separate from your domain entity. It's exactly how you separate a public DTO from a JPA entity. It also gives you a unit-testable contract for "what the model sees".
56291d0de7:
Pruning at the tool makes each result small. It doesn't stop small results from piling up. And some results are unavoidably large, like a policy document or a source file under edit. The next step is to remove results from the history once they've been used.

Chapter 03 section 11 showed the basic broken and fixed versions. In short: never delete a tool_result block. The API rejects any history in which an assistant tool_use id has no matching result in the next user turn. Instead, replace the content of old results with a short placeholder, and keep every block and id.

This section is about the decisions inside that policy. The exam, and real incidents, are about the decisions.
b85d2add9f:
Which results to clear. Oldest first is the default, because the most recent results are the ones the model is still reasoning about.

Count-based retention ("keep the last three tool uses") is simple and predictable. Token-based retention ("keep results until the history is under 30,000 tokens") adapts to result size. But it makes the cut point jump around, which hurts caching. A hybrid many teams use: keep the last N, and also clear any single result larger than a threshold once it's two turns old.
aaf90be0be:
What never to clear. Results the agent needs to keep consulting:

  • a policy document it must check every refund against;
  • the file it's currently editing;
  • memory-tool reads;
  • results from tools that are expensive or non-deterministic to call again (web search, a slow mainframe query, a paid data API).

These go on an exclusion list. If a large result must stay, ask whether it belongs in the system prompt or a facts block instead. There it's stable and cacheable.
13eb6af67a: What the placeholder says. "[cleared]" is legal. "[tool result cleared after use; call get_order again if you need it]" is better. It tells the model the information existed, and how to get it back. Without that, a model that sees a gap may assume the call failed and retry immediately. Or, worse, it may assume the result was empty.
a69d8c37a3: Whether to clear inputs too. Tool inputs are usually small. Occasionally they aren't, as with a write_file call whose input is the whole file. Then clearing them saves as much as clearing the result. The cost is that the model can no longer see what it asked for. That matters if it's about to ask again.
4473fbc308:
Thinking blocks. Say you use extended or adaptive thinking with tools. When you post the tool result, the API requires the thinking block that preceded the tool_use to be sent back unmodified, with its signature. So client-side edits must never rewrite or reorder thinking blocks in the current tool cycle.

On the 5.5-generation models, editing earlier turns client-side can also invalidate thinking blocks in every later assistant turn. New accounts from 31 August 2026 get a rejection, not a silent drop, when an invalidated block is replayed (check the docs, "keeping the prefix unchanged").

This is one of the strongest practical reasons to let the server do the editing (section 08). Server-side context management never invalidates thinking blocks on those models.
50eba9e2bd: Keep your stored history complete, even when you send a cleared copy. Clearing is a view over the log, not a mutation of it. The full transcript is your audit trail and your replay fixture (chapter 12). It's also your evidence when a customer disputes what the agent said. In Spring terms, the conversation table is append-only, and the "request builder" produces a projection of it per call.
ffbc3682b3: The API can apply clearing for you, on the server's copy of the prompt, through the context_management request field. At the time of writing it's a beta, enabled with the context-management-2025-06-27 header. It offers two strategies. (Verified against the documentation in October 2026. Check the docs before shipping, because beta names and defaults change.)
9894b5432c:
The response reports what happened in context_management.applied_edits. For tool clearing, that's cleared_tool_uses and cleared_input_tokens. For thinking, it's cleared_thinking_turns and cleared_input_tokens. When streaming, the same object arrives in the final message_delta event.

Log these per turn. Your stored history still holds the full payloads, so these fields are the only record of what the model actually saw.
767cf8ed20: Your request still carries everything. You send the full history every turn, and the server clears it again. For the cleared parts you pay in bandwidth and request-size limits, not input tokens. If request size is itself a problem (very long sessions), you need client-side clearing or compaction as well.
424870f78c: It is idempotent per request. The same history with the same edit config produces the same cleared prompt. That keeps the prefix stable between turns, as long as the cut point doesn't move. Count-based keep moves the cut point by one tool use per turn. That's what clear_at_least is for.
c042da3072: Token counting sees it. Pass the same context_management to the beta count_tokens call. You get the post-edit count plus original_input_tokens. A preflight check can then decide whether server-side clearing alone will keep you under your working limit.
7bf727c7e1: Memory gets a warning. If the memory tool (chapter 03) is in the request alongside context editing, Claude gets an automatic warning as the context nears the clearing threshold. It can then save what it needs to memory files before results are cleared. This is the documented pairing: clearing keeps the window small, and memory keeps what must survive.
dc4515ccbd:
Prompt caching (chapter 15) reads an unchanged prefix at roughly a tenth of the base input price. It writes a new prefix at a premium: 1.25 times base for the five-minute cache at the time of writing (check current pricing).

Clearing a block at position p changes the prefix from p onward. So everything after p must be written to the cache again. The saving, on the other hand, is a tenth of the cleared tokens on each remaining turn.

Whether clearing pays depends on how much you clear relative to how much you must rewrite, and on how many turns are left. Example 06_clear_vs_cache.py computes it for a 120,000-token cached history:
5dfb6e03fa:
Small clears deep in a cached prefix almost never pay back. You rewrite a large suffix to save a little per turn. Large clears that remove most of the suffix pay back within a couple of turns.

That's why clear_at_least exists. It's also why a sensible configuration clears in large, infrequent batches (a high trigger, a meaningful minimum) rather than trimming a little every turn.

Without caching, the arithmetic changes completely. Every cleared token is saved on every later turn at full price, and frequent small clears are fine.

The exam angle is the general rule: any edit to an earlier part of the prompt invalidates the cache from that point. So context policies and caching policies must be designed together.
990574b695:
Clearing removes payloads but leaves the skeleton: every turn, every reasoning paragraph, every placeholder. On a long enough run, the skeleton alone is too large. And stale reasoning about superseded plans is itself a source of drift.

Compaction replaces the older history with a summary, then continues from there. It's lossy by construction, which is what sections 10 and 11 are about. This section covers the mechanics. There are now four variants.
2aaf0803eb:
You add an edit of type compact_20260112 to context_management, with the compact-2026-01-12 beta. When the input crosses the trigger, the API summarises the conversation. It returns a compaction content block in the response, and generates the reply from the summary onward.

You append response.content to your history as usual. On later requests, the API drops everything before the compaction block. The documented parameters, verified in October 2026:
3ef0730903:
Two details are where teams go wrong.

Billing: with the beta enabled, every response carries usage.iterations, a list of entries typed "compaction" or "message". The top-level input_tokens and output_tokens exclude the compaction iteration. So a cost dashboard that reads only the top-level fields under-reports exactly the turns where compaction ran. Sum the iterations. Example 07_compaction_threshold_sim.py shows the gap: on the compacting turn, the top-level usage is 44 tokens and the billed total is about 60,000.

Caching: put a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. Then, when compaction replaces the history, the system prompt is still read from cache, and only the summary is written. You can also put a breakpoint on the compaction block itself, to cache the summary for later turns.
301cc5ade3:
The default summarisation prompt varies by model. The documentation quotes one that asks for "a summary of the transcript... to provide continuity so you can continue to make progress towards solving the task in a future context". It includes state, next steps and learnings, wrapped in <summary> tags.

Notice what it doesn't ask for: exact identifiers, amounts, dates and their sources. If your task depends on those, you have options. Write instructions that demand them. (Remember they replace the default prompt, so include the continuity request too.) Or keep them in a facts block outside the history. Or both. Section 10 measures the difference.
184acbdc35:
The newer variant lets you ask for a summary when you decide, for example at a phase boundary, instead of at a token threshold. It uses the compact-2026-09-04 beta and a top-level compaction parameter, {"type": "summarize"}. Optional instructions must be non-blank, up to 16,384 characters, and replace the default prompt.

The API summarises every message in the request and generates no reply. It returns a single compaction block with content and a signature, with stop_reason: "compaction". The top-level usage is zero. The cost shows up in usage.iterations.
b6f906ab65:
To continue, replace the summarised messages with an assistant message containing that block, unchanged, signature included. It goes in as the first message. Send exactly one compaction block on every later request, with the same beta header. If any summarised message remains in front of the block, the request fails with a 400 (compaction_block_misplaced).

You can't combine the compaction parameter with context_management on the same request. Send the same system and tools as the rest of the conversation.

To compact again later, send compaction again. The new block summarises the old summary plus everything since. The documentation also advises telling the summariser, in your instructions, not to call tools.
0710a89f4f:
Claude Code compacts automatically as a session approaches its context limit. It also gives you three commands that map onto this chapter:

  • /compact summarises now, and accepts focus instructions (for example /compact keep the failing test names, the file paths changed, and the open TODOs);
  • /clear discards the conversation and starts fresh, which is the right move between unrelated tasks;
  • /context shows what's occupying the window (system prompt, tools, MCP servers, memory files, messages).

The Claude Agent SDK compacts automatically as well. Exact thresholds, settings and output formats change between releases, so check the docs. But the exam-level distinctions are stable. /compact keeps the task and loses detail. /clear keeps nothing. And CLAUDE.md content is reloaded from disk, not summarised. That's why durable project rules belong there and not in the conversation.
d5235f0f9c:
Earlier SDK versions offered client-side compaction in the tool runner: compaction_control with enabled, context_token_threshold defaulting to 100,000, and an optional summary model and summary_prompt.

At the time of writing, the documentation recommends server-side compaction instead. compaction_control survives only in the TypeScript and Ruby SDKs, and it's deprecated there. It was removed from the Python SDK in v1.0. With the Python tool runner, you pass the compact_20260112 edit in context_management.

If you see compaction_control in an older codebase or an exam option, recognise it as the legacy client-side mechanism (check the docs).
e231c4ea39:
A summary is a model's opinion of what mattered, written for a reader it imagines. Summaries are good at gist: who wants what, what happened, what's next. They're bad at specifics, because specifics are exactly what compression removes.

CCAR-F 5.1 names the casualties: numbers, dates, percentages and stated expectations. Add identifiers and provenance (where each fact came from), and you have the list that matters in support, billing, compliance and incident work.
ee51d7ff80: Example 08_summary_loss.py makes the loss concrete. Five turns of a lost-parcel case contain twelve specifics: an order id, two amounts, four dates, a tracking number, a ticket id, two source labels and a policy version. A gist summary, of the kind a default prompt produces, reads well:
c5a4f62412:
Every one of the twelve is gone. The summary isn't wrong. It's just useless for the next step, which is to refund a specific amount on a specific order, citing a specific policy.

An agent continuing from it will either re-query everything, wasting the turns compaction was meant to save. Or, worse, it will fill the gaps with plausible values: "the order total of $179.99", when the customer said $189.99 and the system says $179.99. That discrepancy is itself a fact worth keeping.
3b952b0f09: Three properties of the loss are worth knowing, for design and for the exam.
0e3e57be53: It compounds. The second compaction summarises the first summary plus new turns. A detail that survived once as "about $190" becomes "a refund" the second time. Long-running agents that rely on repeated compaction alone drift towards generalities. CCAR-F 5.4's "typical patterns instead of specific classes" is this effect in a code-exploration setting.
b1b4ef9bc3: Provenance goes first. Summaries merge claims from different sources into one voice. "The carrier says LOST, declared 2026-09-30" and "the customer says it was promised by 2026-10-02" become "the parcel was lost". When sources conflict, the summary picks one, silently. CCAR-F 5.6 tests the fix: keep claim-to-source mappings as structured data that survives summarisation.
9201db52ed: Specific instructions survive no better than specific facts. "Never offer a credit above $50 without supervisor approval", stated in turn 2, can come out of a summary as "follow credit policy". That's the drift mechanism of section 13. It's why rules belong in the system prompt, which no compaction touches.
51dcf295b9:
If you write your own summariser, or pass instructions to server-side compaction, ask for structure rather than prose. And name the classes of specifics. A prompt that works well in practice has four parts:

  • the purpose: continuity for the same task;
  • the required sections: goal, state, decisions with reasons, open actions, next step;
  • a verbatim list of specifics, with sources;
  • constraints: no tool calls, no new facts, flag conflicts.

Then audit it. Extract specifics from the input with deterministic patterns. Extract them from the summary. Fail or fall back if any are missing, exactly as audit() does in example 08. An audit is cheap and deterministic, and it catches the failure before it reaches the next window.
2c91a45334:
A better summary prompt reduces loss. It doesn't eliminate it, and it still depends on a model call getting things right every time.

The structural fix, which CCAR-F 5.1 names directly, is to keep the facts that must survive outside the history. They live in a block your harness owns and rebuilds on every call. Compaction and clearing operate on the history. The facts block isn't in the history, so they can't touch it.

Chapter 03 section 06 introduced the idea. Here's how to build one that holds up in production.
3b0cb136d9:
Structure. A dictionary of named facts. Each has a value, a source, the turn it was recorded, and optionally an as-of date. Use JSON or XML inside a tagged block (<case_facts>), so the model can tell it apart from conversation and your code can parse and validate it.

Keep it small: a few hundred to a couple of thousand tokens. A facts block that grows to 20,000 tokens has become a second history.
d967dd1659:
Who writes it. There are two routes, and you want both.

The harness writes facts from systems of record directly: the order total from get_order, the plan from the CRM. It can parse tool results deterministically.

The model proposes facts it learned in conversation, like the amount the customer says they paid, or the date they were promised. It does this through a record_fact tool. Your code validates the proposal (type, format, allowed keys) before writing it. The model never edits the block directly.
0cc91ccd9d: Conflicts. When a new value disagrees with a held value, don't overwrite silently. Record the conflict, with both values and both sources. Let the system of record win for the working value. Render the open conflict in the block, so the model can address it: "you mentioned $189.99; our records show $179.99 including a discount". Example 09_case_facts_block.py does exactly this.
016b37b339:
Placement. Render the block at the start of the request. Either put it in the system prompt, after the static rules so the static part stays cacheable, or at the top of the first user turn. The model reads both positions reliably (section 12), and both survive any history edit.

If the block changes often and you cache aggressively, put it after your last cache breakpoint. Then a change doesn't invalidate the rules and tool definitions before it.
6aef330235:
In Spring, the facts block is a small entity keyed by conversation id, with a JSON column (or a Redis hash). Your tool handlers and a record_fact endpoint write it. The same request builder that assembles the system prompt renders it.

Treat it like any other piece of case state. Validate on write. Version it. Include it in your audit log per turn, so you can reconstruct exactly what the model was told.
0548ab9e07:
Stem: a long support session is compacted (or progressively summarised). Afterwards, the agent offers the wrong refund amount, or asks again for an order number the customer already gave.

Right answer: keep transactional facts (ids, amounts, dates, stated expectations) in a persistent structured block. Include it in every request, outside the summarised history.

Distractors:

  • "summarise more often" compounds the loss;
  • "use a larger context window so you never summarise" costs in price and attention, and the session will still eventually need it;
  • "tell the model to remember the amount" fails because a summary of that instruction is subject to the same loss;
  • "lower the temperature" is irrelevant.
67b3d8bae8:
The 2023 "lost in the middle" study put a single relevant document at different positions among many irrelevant ones, and measured question-answering accuracy. Accuracy was highest with the relevant document first or last, and lowest in the middle: a U-shaped curve. It fell as the number of distractor documents grew.

Later models, Claude included, are much better at long-context retrieval than the models in that paper. Don't assume any particular curve for a current model without measuring it.

Two conclusions have held up, though, and both are design rules rather than model trivia: position affects how reliably material is used, and irrelevant material makes every position worse.
95b29561b3:
Anthropic's long-context prompting guidance turns this into concrete layout advice (check the docs for current wording):

  • Put long documents and inputs near the top of the prompt, above your instructions and examples.
  • Put the query and instructions at the end. The guidance reports this can noticeably improve response quality on complex, multi-document inputs.
  • Wrap each document in tags with its source and metadata (<document><source>…</source><document_content>…).
  • For long documents, ask the model to first extract the relevant quotes into tags, then answer from them. That focuses attention on the parts that matter.
1035b29527:
Apply the same reasoning to an agent's history. In a long session, the start (system prompt, facts block, original task) and the end (the latest turns) are read reliably. The middle is a long run of tool results and reasoning.

A value that lives only in the middle, such as an account id mentioned once at turn 6 of 40, is the most likely to be overlooked. It's also the most likely to be summarised away. That's the second argument for the facts block: it moves exactly those values from the middle to the start.

CCAR-F 5.1 phrases the same idea as "place key findings summaries at the beginning" of aggregated inputs. Say a coordinator passes ten sub-agent reports to a synthesis step. Put a short table of key findings with sources first, the full reports after it, and the synthesis instruction last.
ce86f9b133:
Example 10_placement.py is a layout linter you can put in a test suite. Given a list of request sections with sizes and kinds, it flags critical content whose midpoint falls in the middle half. It also flags a query that isn't at the end. It encodes the rule, not a model property, and that's exactly what you can test deterministically.

Placement interacts with caching. Long, stable documents at the top are also the ideal cache prefix, and the volatile question at the end sits outside it. The layout that helps attention is the layout that helps cost.
e786286901:
Chapter 17 covers where instructions go (system versus user turn). The short version for context engineering: durable rules and role go in the system prompt, which no context edit touches. Per-task instructions and the question go at the end of the user turn, after the material they refer to.

The exam's "lost in the middle" questions usually describe a critical value or instruction that appears once, mid-way through a long input, and gets ignored. The fix moves it to the start (facts, key-findings summary) or repeats it near the end. It isn't "use a bigger model".
8dedef5118:
Drift is the slow version of failure. The agent followed a rule at turn 5 and breaks it at turn 45. It was investigating a specific failing cell, and now it's describing "typical transport issues". It was asked to change one module, and it's refactoring three. Nothing threw an exception.

There are three mechanisms, and they need different fixes.
425b2d80a0: Dilution. The rule is a fixed number of tokens in a window that grows every turn. Example 15_drift_detector.py prints the share. A 20-token rule set is 0.23% of the window after one 9,000-token turn, and 0.04% after six. Share alone doesn't decide adherence. But share and distance from the current turn both move the wrong way as the session grows. And long runs of tool output between the rule and the decision are exactly where models are least reliable.
0145c4547f: Contamination. The history contains examples of the agent's own earlier outputs, and models continue patterns they see. If turns 10 to 20 contain long, unformatted answers produced while a tool was misbehaving, turn 21 is more likely to produce another. Stale plans have the same effect. A plan written at turn 3 and superseded at turn 15 is still in the window, and still persuasive.
6b737fa4b9:
The fixes follow from the mechanisms.

Durable rules belong in the system prompt (or CLAUDE.md in Claude Code). It's sent on every call, sits at the start, and is never compacted. Rules that come up mid-conversation should be promoted into the facts block or the system prompt by your harness, not left as a chat message.

At phase boundaries (after investigation, before action; after each sub-task), append a short reminder to the next user turn that points at the standing rules. A reminder is a pointer, not a second copy of the whole system prompt.

And "follow the rule" is a probabilistic property. So detect violations with deterministic checks on outputs: a regex for card numbers, a check that every customer-facing answer cites a source id, a diff check that edits stay within the files named in the task.
f4f55f1cd7:
The detector tracks a sliding violation rate over the last six outputs. It also tracks the distance in tokens between the rules and the current turn. If either crosses a threshold, it triggers a reminder. A rate that stays high after a reminder triggers the stronger response in section 17: a fresh session from exported state. That escalation (detect, remind, restart) is the operational form of drift prevention.

Note also the CCAR-F 5.4 framing. A long code-exploration session starts giving answers about "typical patterns" rather than the specific classes it found earlier. The fixes the exam wants are a scratchpad file of findings, delegating further exploration to sub-agents, and summarising key findings before the next phase. All of them move specifics out of the decaying middle of the history.
2fedb75e63: Chapter 01 treats sub-agents as an architecture. Chapter 03 section 14 treats them as an agent pattern, with the brief-and-result contract and the Claude Agent SDK code. This section is about the one thing the 6.1 objective cares about: sub-agents as a context isolation mechanism, and the accounting that decides when isolation pays.
3057e85c44:
A sub-agent is a separate model conversation with its own window. The parent sends a brief. The sub-agent runs as many turns as it needs, reading files, logs or search results into its window. It returns a short result, and its window is discarded. The parent's window grows by the brief and the result only.

Example 11_subagent_isolation.py runs the same three-log investigation both ways with the fake client. It records every call's input size:
1ed9a1aea7:
Three readings of those numbers.

Total tokens did not go down. The sub-agent read the same logs and paid for them, plus its own brief. Across both agents, the delegated run used slightly more. Isolation isn't a way to read less. It's a way to read in a window you throw away.

The lead's window is clean. Its largest call is 109 tokens instead of 18,125. That difference persists for every later turn of the lead's session. If the lead runs thirty more turns, the single-agent design pays for 18,000 tokens of logs thirty more times, and keeps them in the lead's attention.

The bulk work ran on a cheaper model. Reading logs for one error is Haiku work. The lead's synthesis may be Opus work. Isolation lets each window use the right model.
1b538b7784:
From this accounting, the rule for when isolation helps falls out in four conditions.

  • The sub-task must be verbose. It generates much more context than its conclusion: reading many files to find one call site, scanning logs for one error.
  • It must be separable. You can write a complete brief without the parent's history, because the sub-agent inherits nothing. (In the Agent SDK, the Task tool's prompt string is the only channel.)
  • Its result must fit a contract: fields, limits and format. That keeps the result small, and the parent can rely on its shape.
  • Ideally it's parallelisable, so several sub-agents run at once and wall-clock time drops too.

When the sub-task is a two-call lookup, isolation costs a model call and a lossy hand-off, and saves nothing.
23b605cb09:
Two failure modes matter for the exam.

The first is the under-specified brief ("check the logs for the issue we discussed"). It gives an isolated agent nothing to work with. The fix is a self-contained brief with goal, known facts, constraints and output contract. Chapter 03 section 14 has the broken and fixed code.

The second is the unbounded result. A sub-agent told to "summarise the logs" may return 3,000 tokens of excerpts, which defeats the isolation. The result contract is where the context saving is actually enforced. Validate it in code, and reject or truncate oversize results.
c3930fda51:
Claude Code shows the same economics. Its built-in Explore sub-agent, and any custom sub-agents in .claude/agents/, run searches and reads in their own context and hand back a summary. So a broad question like "where is retry logic configured across these services" doesn't leave a hundred Grep hits in your main session. A skill with context: fork does the same for a skill's work.

In a long interactive session, delegating exploration this way often makes the difference. One session stays sharp for hours. The other needs /compact every twenty minutes.
887a2ece57:
Some work doesn't fit in one window, however well you prune: migrating six services, triaging two hundred tickets, reconciling a month of roaming records. Some work must survive a crash, a deploy or a human going home.

Both need state that lives outside the window, which a fresh window can start from. In section 02's terms, this is write-back. Before anything leaves the window, the part that matters is written to durable storage.
2ddfe59cb0:
Chapter 03 covers the memory tool (model-driven files under /memories for cross-session memory) and structured progress notes for multi-window tasks. Here the focus is on making a state file robust. That's what CCAR-F 5.4 means by "structured state export for crash recovery" and "scratchpad files".

Example 12_scratchpad_state.py runs a six-service migration. It crashes the process after three, then resumes in a new process from the file alone.
cf00592815: Invariant-checked on every write. No item is both done and pending. Every blocked item has a reason. Ids match a known set. A model-maintained file will eventually contain a contradiction. The harness should reject that write rather than resume from it.
727ba33f04: Decisions with reasons. "porting: wait for vendor SDK 5.x (ticket VEN-221)". Decisions are what a fresh window is most likely to re-argue, and the reason is what stops it.
e5a210de90: Verifiable against reality. Where possible, "done" should be checkable: the commit exists, the build passed, the case is closed in the CRM. The next window should verify a sample, not trust the file blindly.
d7bbf97834:
Who writes the file is a design choice.

The model can maintain it through a tool: a update_progress tool, the memory tool, or Claude Code editing a PROGRESS.md or using its TODO list. That captures what the model judged important. The harness can maintain it from events (tool results, completed steps). That captures what actually happened. Robust systems use the harness for the facts of progress, and the model for judgements and notes.

In a Spring Batch mindset, the state file is the job repository's execution context. It's small, structured, committed at each chunk boundary, and the only thing a restart needs.
5f7d6597c0:
"Stuffing" means putting the whole corpus into the prompt: all policies, the whole manual, every document in the case. "Retrieval" means fetching, per query, only the parts relevant to it.

With 1M-token windows, stuffing is often possible, and sometimes right. So the question is no longer "does it fit". It's "what does each option cost, and what does each get wrong".
5af5690b21:
Example 13_retrieval_vs_stuffing.py uses a 60-document policy corpus of about 90,000 tokens, and the question "Is the express fee refundable when a parcel is lost?".

Keyword retrieval returns three documents, two of which contain the answer, for about 4,500 tokens. Stuffing sends 90,000 tokens on every call. At ten calls per conversation and five thousand conversations a day, the difference is roughly 4.3 billion input tokens a day, before caching.
a8dba3e979:
For agents there's a third option, and it usually beats both: just-in-time retrieval by the agent itself. Keep lightweight references in context (file paths, document ids, URLs, table names). Give the agent tools to fetch content when a decision needs it: Glob and Grep before Read in Claude Code, or search_kb then get_document(id, section) in a support agent.

This is progressive disclosure. The agent sees a map first and loads territory on demand. Its costs are extra turns, and the risk that the agent doesn't think to look. Good tool descriptions and a short index in the system prompt reduce that risk.
c8ef8034d5:
Whatever you retrieve, keep the source id attached to each chunk in the prompt, and require the model to cite it. That's what makes the answer checkable. It's also the provenance that a later summary must preserve (section 10).

Chunk boundaries matter too. A chunk that splits a policy clause from its exception produces confident wrong answers. Chapter 09 and the CCAR-P guide cover chunking, contextual retrieval and hybrid search in depth. For 6.1, the point is that retrieval is a context-management decision first and a search problem second.
e31b5279e6:
Sooner or later, a session degrades despite everything above. The agent repeats a call it already made. It answers with generalities. It breaks a rule after a reminder. Or the history is simply past any useful size.

The question is how to recover without losing the work. There are three options, and the exam distinguishes them.
3a4c4b9e80: Keep going and compact. Right when the session is healthy but long: the task is the same, the recent turns matter, and the facts block and state file protect specifics. Wrong when the history itself is the problem, contaminated with a bad plan, a wrong value, or a superseded task. The summary will faithfully carry the contamination forward.
cfac4b8156: Resume the old session. In the Agent SDK and Claude Code, resuming restores the transcript. Right when little time has passed and nothing outside has changed. Risky when files, tickets or data changed since: the resumed agent's tool results are stale, and it doesn't know. CCAR-F 1.7 says it directly. Starting fresh with a summary is often more reliable than resuming with stale tool results. If you do resume, tell the agent what changed.
1c832f0189: Start a fresh session from exported state. Right when the session has degraded. Export structured state (facts with sources, done, pending, decisions, next step). Archive the transcript for audit. Start a new session whose first message is the brief plus the state. The new window has the specifics, none of the noise, and no contaminated reasoning.
0cfcb1cfc0:
Example 14_long_session_recovery.py implements the third option with explicit signals. After each turn, the harness checks three conditions:

  • input over the working limit;
  • the same tool called with the same input three times;
  • a violated standing rule (an answer without a source id).

When any of them fires, it exports state and starts a new session:
7e28f8714e:
In Claude Code, the same decision is between /compact (keep going), --resume or --continue (restore a session), and /clear after writing state to a file the next session reads (fresh start).

Here's a practical habit for long coding sessions. Before /clear, ask Claude to write the current plan, decisions and remaining TODOs to a file. Then start the next session with "read PLAN.md and continue". CLAUDE.md is reloaded automatically, so project rules come back without effort.
f33c46d0c4:
Example 16_context_policy.py applies the full ladder to a ten-turn tool session. Each turn adds a tool result of 3,000 to 12,000 tokens, and about 2,500 tokens of reasoning. The working budget is 25,000 tokens. The hard ceiling for a compacted history is 40,000.

The policy runs after each turn:

  • if under budget, do nothing;
  • otherwise, clear all but the last two results;
  • if still over budget, compact to a facts block plus summary plus the last tool exchange;
  • if even that is over the ceiling, start a new window from state.
90608c6505:
Walk it turn by turn.

Turns 1 to 3 stay under budget, and nothing happens. A policy that acts before it must is a policy that pays cache rewrites for nothing.

Turn 4 crosses budget at 36,139. Clearing old results would leave about 26,000, because the reasoning paragraphs aren't tool results. So clearing alone isn't enough, and the policy compacts to 11,566: facts block, summary, last exchange.

Turn 6 crosses again. This time clearing is enough (32,632 to 23,635), because most of the growth since compaction is tool output. Turn 7 needs compaction again, because reasoning has piled up. Turns 9 and 10 are handled by clearing alone.

Over ten turns, the policy compacted twice and cleared three times. Every request passed the pairing validator. The history never exceeded 37,000 tokens.
190db98401:
Two lessons generalise.

First, what accumulates decides which tool works. Tool output yields to clearing. Reasoning and conversation yield only to compaction. Measure both in your traces.

Second, the cheapest sufficient action is the right one. Compaction loses detail and costs a model call. So it should run only when clearing can't get under budget, which is exactly the order in chapter 03's ladder.
88e52cc9e0:
All of the techniques meet in one component: the thing that builds each request. In most codebases this logic is scattered. There's a truncation in one tool, a summary call in a controller, a facts string concatenated somewhere.

Pull it into a single context manager, and it becomes testable and observable. It's the same reason you'd centralise retry policy rather than sprinkle try/catch loops through services.
dfad885f3e: The Java shape is the same. It fits naturally as a Spring bean, with the policy as configuration. If you use Spring AI, its chat-memory advisors give you a message window and persistence. The facts block, the clearing exclusions and the audit of summaries are still yours to write, because they're domain decisions.
5919f46ac6:
Test it like any other policy component.

  • Unit tests feed synthetic histories and assert on the actions taken and the pairing validity of the output. The companion examples are effectively these tests.
  • A property test checks that no sequence of appends and builds ever produces an invalid history.
  • A replay test runs recorded production sessions through a new policy offline, and compares token counts and actions before you deploy it.
edef0d8e03: Each of these has shown up in real systems, and most show up as distractors. The table gives the shape. The code below covers the ones whose fix isn't obvious from the table.
4b797ed0b5: Each scenario describes a symptom and four options. Name the mechanism (bloat, drift, detail loss, placement, contamination) before you read the options. The right answer changes what is in the window.
5db7bc8df6: The mechanism is detail loss in summarisation. B moves the specifics out of the region that summarisation rewrites, so they survive every compaction. A compounds the loss (summaries of summaries). C postpones the problem and raises cost and latency per turn, and the session will still need compacting eventually. D asks the model to remember something that's no longer in its window once the summary dropped it.
99b0d77945: The bloat comes from one tool, and it's visible on the turn the result arrives. So pruning at the source is the cheapest and least lossy fix. It also improves the turn where the result is read. A treats the symptom later, and lossily. C changes price per token, not tokens, and may reduce quality. D is an arbitrary cap that stops investigations rather than shrinking them.
6daa727292: Any change to an earlier part of the prompt invalidates the cache from that point. Clearing a little every turn pays a cache write on a large suffix each time, to save a small read cost. clear_at_least exists for exactly this. B, C and D aren't how the feature works.
49472a3e9f: The critical material sits in the least reliably used position. And the question is read before the material it refers to. A applies the documented long-context layout. B adds noise. C affects output length, not input use. D loses cross-contract reasoning, which the exceptions may need, and still buries nothing less.
b5c7aae0af: This is context degradation in a long session (CCAR-F 5.4). B combines the documented remedies: write-back to a scratchpad, isolation of verbose exploration, phase summaries, and a controlled compaction or reset that carries state. A doesn't change the window. C is maximal bloat. D loses the findings along with the noise.
399987acef: Isolation saves context only if the result is small. "Summarise" invites a long result. What keeps the parent's window small is a contract with fields, provenance and a size limit, enforced in code. A is false: sub-agents have their own windows. C abandons isolation. D hopes for brevity instead of requiring it.
